ELIOS – AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring & Predictive Simulation System
ELIOS is an intelligent astronaut healthcare platform designed to enhance crew safety and medical preparedness during space exploration missions. By integrating AI-driven health simulations, physiological monitoring, and predictive analysis, ELIOS aims to address the challenges of maintaining astronaut health in isolated and demanding space environments.

The system monitors essential physiological parameters, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, body temperature, and other vital indicators. It features six interconnected astronaut profiles within a shared spacecraft environment, ensuring that simulated medical events and mission conditions are synchronized across the entire crew.

ELIOS incorporates AI-assisted simulation to model how medical emergencies, physiological abnormalities, and prolonged exposure to adverse conditions can affect astronauts over time. It allows users to trigger mission events, observe evolving health parameters, fast-forward simulations, and identify potentially critical conditions through an interactive monitoring dashboard.

The platform also supports persistent health records across sessions and is designed with future wearable-device integration in mind, enabling the possibility of collecting real-world biometric data.
details:
ELIOS — An Intelligent Space Crew Health Monitoring and Mission Support System

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

ELIOS is a space-based crew health monitoring and mission support system designed to simulate how astronauts' physical and psychological wellbeing can be monitored during long-duration space missions. It features two mission environments: the International Space Station (ISS) and a Mars habitat.

The system includes 12 fictional astronaut profiles, with six crew members assigned to each environment. It monitors simulated physiological indicators such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, body temperature and blood pressure. It also includes health histories, medical records, sleep and wellbeing information, and an interactive ECG display.

ELIOS allows users to change environmental conditions, simulate mission incidents and observe how these changes may affect crew health. Its Intelligence Layer analyses available readings and trends, identifies potential concerns, and explains why certain indicators have been flagged.

The platform also includes mission time controls, radiation monitoring, environmental telemetry, crew wellbeing analysis, medical report generation and a guided tutorial. Its Mars mode considers the communication delay between Earth and Mars, demonstrating why astronauts on distant missions may need more independent onboard support.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

  • Continuous monitoring: Provides a centralised view of crew health indicators and mission conditions.
  • Early awareness: Identifies unusual readings and changes in health trends that may need attention.
  • Mission preparedness: Allows users to simulate emergencies and environmental changes before considering how a crew might respond.
  • Psychological wellbeing: Includes sleep, mood, cognitive performance, resilience and crew cohesion indicators.
  • Better communication: Demonstrates how medical reports can be prepared for communication with a flight surgeon, including when communication delays are present.
  • Educational value: Helps users understand the challenges of human spaceflight through interactive simulations.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of ELIOS is to demonstrate how intelligent monitoring and data analysis could support astronaut health and safety during future long-duration missions.

As humanity explores the Moon, Mars and destinations farther from Earth, astronauts may face challenges such as radiation exposure, isolation, reduced gravity, communication delays and limited access to immediate medical assistance.

ELIOS aims to demonstrate how a unified mission-support platform could help crews understand their health information, recognise potential problems and make better-informed decisions.

In the long term, the concept could inspire the development of more advanced spaceflight health-monitoring systems that combine medical information, environmental data and intelligent analysis.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware and software were used?

Programming languages and technologies:

  • HTML5 — structure of the application.
  • CSS3 — interface design, animations, visual effects and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript — application logic, simulations, data processing and interactive features.
  • Three.js — interactive 3D space-station visualisation.
  • HTML Canvas API — ECG displays and visual effects.
  • Web Audio API — procedural sound effects and ambient audio.

Data and software technologies:

  • Browser local storage — retaining simulated crew records and user check-ins locally.
  • NASA DONKI and NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center data sources — space-weather information when available.
  • wheretheiss.at — ISS position information when available.
  • Web browsers such as Google Chrome — running the application.

Hardware:

The prototype was developed and tested using a standard computer or laptop. It does not currently require specialised medical sensors, wearable devices or dedicated aerospace hardware.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

ELIOS combines several different areas of technology into one interactive spaceflight operations platform.

Instead of displaying health readings in a conventional dashboard, it connects crew health, environmental conditions and mission events within two distinct simulated habitats.

One of its most creative features is the Intelligence Layer, which goes beyond displaying numbers by explaining potential trends and why certain readings deserve attention.

The ISS and Mars environments also have different visual identities and ambient soundscapes. The application includes an interactive 3D station, animated backgrounds, procedural sound effects, mission simulations and a guided tutorial.

Another innovative aspect is its focus on both physical and psychological wellbeing. It recognises that successful long-duration space missions depend not only on physical health but also on sleep, mental resilience and teamwork.

6. What factors did the team consider during development?

Several important factors were considered:

  1. Astronaut safety: The system was designed around the major challenges of human spaceflight, including radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity changes and hostile environments.
  2. Scientific relevance: The project incorporates spaceflight-related concepts and reference information while distinguishing simulated readings from available external data.
  3. Communication delays: Mars missions may experience significant delays when communicating with Earth, so the platform demonstrates the importance of onboard monitoring and decision support.
  4. User experience: The interface was designed to be interactive, understandable and easy to navigate, with a guided tutorial to introduce its features.
  5. Data privacy: Personal check-ins and records are stored locally in the browser, and the visual colour-screening demonstration processes photographs locally.
  6. Reliability and limitations: The team considered the difference between a working simulation and a real medical system. The health readings, crew profiles and medical decision rules are illustrative and require professional validation before any real-world use.
  7. Adaptability: The platform was designed to support two different mission environments, allowing users to compare the operational challenges of an orbital space station and a Mars habitat.

Conclusion

ELIOS is more than a conventional health dashboard. It is an interactive demonstration of how space medicine, intelligent data analysis, environmental simulation and mission operations could work together to support astronauts during future space exploration. Its ultimate vision is to contribute to a future where astronauts can monitor their wellbeing, understand mission risks and make informed decisions even when Earth is millions of kilometres away.
